analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican cosponsor in March 2025, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would temporarily limit credit card interest rates to 10%, including all finance charges, from now until January 1, 2031. Creditors who knowingly charge more would forfeit all interest on the debt, and borrowers could sue within two years to recover any interest, finance charges, or fees they overpaid. It also bars lenders from using fees to get around the cap and leaves stronger state consumer protections in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry a credit card balance from month to month. Those borrowers, roughly half of cardholders, currently pay interest rates that commonly run above 20%; a 10% cap would cut their interest costs sharply. Borrowers who were overcharged could claw back the money through a private lawsuit.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 10 percentage points, inclusive of all finance charges, through January 1, 2031.
Bars creditors from using fees that are not technically finance charges to evade the cap, and limits the total of such fees to no more than the finance charges assessed.

Creditors who knowingly charge above the cap forfeit the entire interest on the debt, and borrowers can sue within two years to recover the full amount of interest, finance charges, or fees they paid.
Violations carry civil liability under the Truth in Lending Act, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission.
The cap does not preempt state laws that give consumers stronger protections.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks, whose interest revenue on revolving balances is the direct target. Some borrowers could also face tighter credit: lenders who can no longer price high-risk accounts at high rates tend to raise down-payment-like requirements, cut credit lines, or decline riskier applicants.

drawbacks.text: A hard 10% cap limits lenders' ability to price risk. Borrowers with poor credit, who currently pay the highest rates, are the most likely to see credit lines cut or applications denied, since lenders cannot charge them rates that cover their default risk.
The cap is temporary, sunsetting on January 1, 2031, so the relief would lapse unless Congress renews it.
The bill tries to close the common loophole of loading costs into fees, but fee-shifting and new account structures could still erode the benefit at the margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of cardholders who carry a balance, the benefit is large and direct: interest costs that often exceed 20% would be cut to 10%. The main honest tradeoff is credit access for the riskiest borrowers, since lenders cannot charge them rates that reflect their default risk. The bill's anti-evasion language, forfeiture penalty, and private right of action make it harder to sidestep than a plain cap, though its five-year sunset means the relief is not permanent.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor action has followed.

narrative.text: Representative Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 6, 2025, joined by Representative Luna, a Republican, as its sole cosponsor.
The same day, the House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services.
No further action — no committee markup, no vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, credit card issuers: the bill sits in committee with no scheduled action, so current interest rates above 20% continue unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 6, 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no markup or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have consistently opposed federal interest rate caps, which would cut directly into interest revenue on revolving balances; no such campaign appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but that two-member coalition has produced no committee action and no votes to measure the parties by.

industries.note: The bill's core effect is a hard 10% ceiling on interest rates that commonly run above 20%, cutting directly into the interest banks collect on revolving balances. The benefit to cardholders who carry debt comes straight out of issuer revenue, which is why the industry's interest in the bill runs against borrowers'.

These lenders price risk through high APRs; the cap removes that tool, likely pushing them to deny or restrict credit to the riskiest applicants rather than lend at 10%. Borrowers with weak credit could lose access rather than gain cheaper debt.

analysis.trajectory: With only two sponsors, no Republican or Democratic committee leadership support visible, and no markup five months after referral, the bill is likely to sit in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote, as similar rate-cap proposals have in past Congresses. It would need the committee chair to schedule action to move at all.
